page_title: Top 15 French to English Translation Apps You Must Know
meta_description: Great French to English translation apps: 1.Google Translate 2.Word Reference 3.FranGo Others like TripLingo, Reverso are also popular.
content: Skip to content Top 15 French to English Translation Apps You Must Know 2022-09-30 French french French to English translation apps are very helpful when stumbling into a situation where you’re drawing a blank when speaking French. Suppose you’re studying French, planning on traveling in the foreseeable future, watching a French movie, or just starting the process on how to learn french. In that case, a French-to-English translation app can be invaluable. Although having a fluent friend to be your French translator wherever you go would be awesome, no friend is that awesome. if you’re a beginner it becomes especially important to make use of these tools as an English-to-French translation app will drastically improve your vocabulary. Translation apps come with so many gadgets, gizmos, and features but each one has its limits so instead of wasting your valuable time we’ve compiled a comprehensive list of the top 15 French translator apps and everything you need to know about them. Happy learning! Best General Translation App Google Translate Source: Google Translate Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: translate text from an image or handwritingautomatic language recognitionTranslates websites and pdfs and Word documents Let’s start with old Google Translate. I think the majority of us have come across this feature at least once in our lives. Although the app has had a fair bit of criticism in the past, it has made strides in improvement in recent times. One of the features that have improved over the last few years is the text-to-speak function which allows you to play back the audio version of your translation to improve your pronunciation and to make comprehension and communication a bit easier. Although it is important to note you may notice some common translation mistakes in the software. ProsConsGoogle Translate is freeGoogle Translate cannot provide a perfectly accurate translationGoogle Translate is quick.There is no proofreadingGoogle Translate is quick.Google Translate offers no security or confidentiality for your data. WordReference Source: Google Play Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: Only offers translations of words and phrasesResults from native speakersA popular community that’s involved in improving the experience for you. If you’re looking to figure out the nuances and idiomatic phrases of a language then WordReference is the place to go for cultural translations. What’s great about this app is the popular community that’s involved in improving the experience for you. WordReference makes use of a large forum frequented by native speakers where you can follow past conversations searchable by keywords to hopefully answer your question. It should be noted though that users prefer you to attempt to solve your question first and then native French speakers will correct and help you arrive at the right translation. ProsConstakes advantage of questions that have already been answered by membersnot all words have audio pronunciationMakes use of native speakersis not the best place to go for a direct translation of a sentence Not a great catch-all app. Translate Offline Source: Google Play Available On Google Play Key features: Works without internet or dataCompletely freeTranslates voice, photos, and texts If you often run low on data or find yourself in an area with poor quality or no WiFi then Translate Offline can be very useful to you. For travelers, this offline English to French translator app functions without depending on the Internet and can save you the headache of data roaming charges when you travel. Another plus of this app is that it is completely free with an option to buy a full version without ads ProsConsTranslate Offline is freeIntrusive pop-up ads and survey requestsTranslate Offline is a data saverThere is no proofreading FranGo Source: Google Play Available On Google Play, Istore Key features: French keyboard extensionAl Camera Translatoroffers transliteration, Sharing, Favorites, History, and Learning FranGo lets you translate voice, text, photos in many languages to french or vice versa accurately, learning French or other languages more easily. This app features an accurate voice translator which allows you to listen to voice translations in either a male or female voice of your choice. A great aspect of this app is the dialect feature which allows you to switch to different dialects to improve your pronunciation in a practical setting. ProsConsNo login required, safe, friendly use easilyRequires a subscription iTranslate Source: Google Play Available On Google Play, Istore Key features: 5 tools to utilizeAllows sharing with contactsOn-the-spot translations iTranslate offers a five-option toolbar that features text translation, a lens to capture images to translate, voice-to-voice powered by speech, a phrasebook including a collection of commonly used expressions organized by categories, and a tab house that stores tagged favorites, history, and a link to website translation. Users can also share translations with contacts via message or email or save them to other apps on the device. This app is free to try but offers in-app purchase options ranging from $4.99 – $49.99 for premium and pro features. ProsCons5 useful tools to satisfy the mindIn-app purchasesAllow sharing and savingIt may miss common sayings and may fail to capture the meaning of certain phrases.Offline optionsAccuracy seems to depend on how common the word is. Best French-English Translation App Takeeasy Source: IStore Available On Istore Key features: 24/7 assistancePersonalized translationsOutbound life assistant Have you ever wanted a personal translation assistant? Well if Takeeasy you’re one step closer. Takeeasy is a French translator app that uses real humans to give you personalized translations on the go with a 24/7 personal assistant for translating anything you need. Although a free trial call is offered, to be expected it is not a free service. This app costs around $1.99/min and although that sounds expensively daunting, most people will only need to use it for a few minutes at a time, keeping the total cost fairly low. ProsConsNo charge if you hang up in 30 seconds.Pay per minuteFree airtime will be sent monthlyMust have a good connectionShake three times every day to get coupons for free translation. TripLingo Source: TripLingo Available On: Istore Key features: local emergency information, medical phrases and safety tools.currency converter and tip calculatorfree international calls when connected with Wi-Fi If you’re a foreigner visiting an international country this app is specifically targeted at you. TripLingo provides a phrasebook, and tip calculator, helps you to tell the time in French, and even has a Wi-Fi dialer and addition a useful voice translation feature. TripLingo refers to itself as your go-to culture guide to help you make a good first impression as an etiquette tool. A plus with this app is the built-in Wi-Fi dialer which allows you to make free international calls when connected with Wi-Fi. ProsConsA culture guide is useful when navigating hostile conditionsapp crashes most of the time when trying to take wi-fi callsFree calls on wifi to save roaming chargesOther features of this app have known to crashphrasebook including formal, casual and slang options TranslateMe Source: TranslateMe Available On Google Play Key features: Simple and intuitive designVirtually seamless translationsUses the same technology as Google Translate if you prefer a simple and intuitive experience, this French-to-English translation app would be the tool for you. Translate Me is a great option if you need an easy format and plan to be translating in both directions frequently. This app is designed as a layer that’s on top of Google Translate, so it’s no different from Google’s technology From a functionality perspective. This app also features an easy-to-use option that translates source text from a text message meaning you can translate a French text without having to copy and paste. ProsConsSeamless designOnly allows 2 translations a day without a premium subscriptionTranslates text messagesApp is known to crashGoogle Translate is quick.Price can be a bit steep Best Context Translator Microsoft Translator Source: Google Play Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: Useful phrasebook with common phrasesAutomatically integrated with the rest of Microsoft suiteTranslation of conversations across devices Microsoft Translator promises a lot but can it live up to its competition Google Translate? On first inspection, this app may be a bit overwhelming with all its features and it offers virtually the same as google with translations via keyboard, speech, handwriting, and photo. It is important to note the Microsoft translator is already integrated into Outlook, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. This app can be disappointing though as it sometimes even fails to translate the most simple sentences. ProsConsMicrosoft suite integratedMicrosoft text translation doesn’t perform as well as its competition.Translates entire documentsthe translation quality is poorGoogle Translate is quick.shouldn’t be used in a professional context. Reverso Source: IStore Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: Includes examples of use in context.Instant translationsHas an index of millions of words Although this app is designed for large businesses, it is an all-in-one tool that provides you with high-quality translations and helps you improve your language skills seamlessly. Reverso is integrated with AI technology to effortlessly find countless examples in context and understand subtleties between different translations just by entering a word or expression. Although this app is free to use it does offer in-app purchases starting at $6.50 per month. ProsConslooks at the overall meaning of the sentence and provides the most suitable alternative that fits well into the overall meaning.The app does not work as well on desktop use.Reverso allows you to translate a whole sentence by simply copying it into the clipboard. Gives translations with various examples Talk & Translate Source: Google Play is Available On Google Play, Istore Key features: Translations from Collins Dictionaryreal-time voice translationsOffline mode for translations without the internet Talk & Translate is a French to English translation app that works as a real-time voice and text translator with a streamlined user interface. It utilizes Collins Premium dictionaries to translate speech, text, or photos in seconds.this app offers an offline mode so you can avoid paying expensive roaming charges by downloading databases and translations, although it is important to note that the free version does require an active internet connection. A premium subscription to this app offers unlimited translations and no ads but the price may be steep for some at $69.99 per year. ProsConsPick up hard-to-understand accentsSubscriptions information is misleading and difficult to cancel Some translations may be inaccurate Best Speaking Translation App Translate All Languages Source: IStore Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: Share translated words and documents with friends.Detailed historyCopy and delete text with one click Translate All Languages allows users to convert text, voice, speech, and words from French to English (and multiple other languages). Made by experts it offers instant voice and text translations with ease of use in mind and is ideal for beginners. Unlike other apps, you can also copy-paste the translation from the translated text and send it to your friends. ProsConsCompletely free and fastPopup ads are intrusiveEasily copy and paste text anywhereNot as good as Google TranslateSimple and attractive user interface DeepL Source: DeepL Available On Google Play, Istore Key features: Completely freeTranslate whole documentsYour data is secure DeepL may just be one of the best translation apps available. DeepL can capture even the slightest nuances and reproduce them in translation, unlike any other service. This app can translate texts quickly and reliably can outperform the competition by a factor of 3:1 and is completely free. ProsConsservers are always encrypted.the mobile app is more limitedOutperforms the competition by a factor of 3:1 Save words and phrases for future reference Jibbigo Source: CrunchBase Available On website Key features: Unlimited free online usageSupports voice and typed inputSupports offline usage Jibbigo is a French to English translation app that you can use online or offline, making it convenient and ideal when traveling. You can download the offline translators when you don’t have WiFi access and there is free unlimited online use. The app dubs itself as an interpreter in your pocket where you can either speak or type your phrases into the app and then you’ll be given the translations. If you have access to an Internet connection, use the app as much as you like in online mode for free. ProsConsworks for both words and short sentencesTo use in offline mode you will first need to download the selections individually.Shows correct spelling FluentU Source: FluentU Available On: Google Play, Istore Key features: Uses flashcards to learn wordssee example sentences, grammar info, audio pronunciations, and clipsPost-video quizzes, transcripts, and keyword FluentU is known as an immersive language learning app but it also has a strong French-to-English translation feature. This strength lies in its contextual video dictionary. A simple word search will bring up all its possible definitions and forms, as well as common phrases where they appear. It uses definition flashcards which you can save to your vocabulary list and study using personalized quizzes. Prices go from $29.99/month or $239.99/year. ProsConsPersonalized flashcardsMore expensive than the competitionTeaches through native French content.Often uses an unnatural robotic-sounding voice Use Translation Apps to Improve Your French Now that we’ve learned all we can about these French to English apps let’s talk about how you can get the most from these tools. First, of all, it doesn’t have to break the bank. We often believe that a bigger price tag equals a better app, This is very often not the case. As we’ve seen above there are plenty of apps that can meet your needs without even spending a penny (especially if you don’t mind popup ads). The second thing to keep in mind is that it’s not always a good idea to use an app that has too many things going on. Almost every one of these apps offers multiple languages so if you need a French or even a Japanese translator, it’s all under one roof. If you can’t stand having to type out everything you want to say then go for a voice-to-speech translation app so you can get real-time translations by speaking through the app. This function worlds both ways so you can enjoy French podcasts, movies, songs, and so much more under your thumb. If you’re traveling to foreign countries I highly suggest making use of image translations so you can easily translate menus and signage without having to tediously type every word. Start Your Journey with Motoshare Post Views: 6 Introduction Text-to-Speech (TTS) platforms are sophisticated software solutions that leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deep learning to convert written text into natural-sounding spoken audio. Gone are the days of the “robotic” and monotone voices of the early 2000s. In , neural TTS technology has reached a point of “near-human” parity, where machines can replicate the subtle nuances of human emotion, breathing, and cadence. These platforms use Neural Network architectures to analyze text and synthesize waveforms that mirror specific human voice profiles across hundreds of languages and dialects. The importance of TTS tools has surged as digital content consumption shifts toward audio-first formats. They are essential for enhancing accessibility for the visually impaired, localizing video content for global markets without the high cost of traditional voice actors, and powering the next generation of conversational AI in customer service. When choosing a platform, users must evaluate latency (how fast the audio is generated), emotional range (the ability to sound happy, sad, or excited), language diversity, and commercial usage rights. Best for: Content creators (YouTube/TikTok), e-learning developers, software engineers building voice-enabled apps, and enterprise marketing teams. It is a game-changer for businesses looking to scale their audio content production quickly and cost-effectively. Not ideal for: High-end cinematic productions requiring specific, award-winning dramatic performances or ultra-niche regional dialects where AI training data remains sparse. It is also not a replacement for live, interactive human performance in theater or high-stakes sensitive counseling where a human presence is legally or ethically required. Top 10 Text-to-Speech (TTS) Platforms 1 — ElevenLabs ElevenLabs has solidified its position as the industry leader in emotional and high-fidelity speech synthesis. It is designed for creators and developers who require the most realistic voices available, offering a level of “expressive” AI that was previously thought impossible. Key features: Voice Lab: Create entirely new synthetic voices or clone existing ones from short clips. Speech-to-Speech: Convert one voice’s delivery into another while maintaining the original’s emotion. Multilingual v2 model supporting 29+ languages with automatic language detection. High-resolution audio output (up to 44.1kHz). Instant Voice Cloning requiring as little as 60 seconds of audio data. Advanced “Stability” and “Clarity” sliders to fine-tune vocal performance. Professional Voice Cloning (PVC) for verified users to create 1:1 digital twins. Pros: Unrivaled emotional intelligence; voices can whisper, shout, or sound sarcastic. Extremely fast API response times, making it viable for real-time applications. Cons: Higher pricing tiers for professional-grade voice cloning features. Character-based billing can become expensive for long-form audiobook production. Security & compliance: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR compliant, SSO for enterprise, and strictly enforced voice cloning ethics policies. Support & community: Extensive documentation, a very active Discord community, and priority support for “Scale” and “Enterprise” tiers. 2 — Murf.ai Murf.ai is a professional-grade “voiceover studio” in the cloud. It is designed for businesses, educators, and podcasters who need to create polished audio for presentations and marketing videos without needing a professional recording setup. Key features: Murf Studio: A comprehensive web-based editor that syncs voiceovers with video and images. Over 120+ high-quality voices in 20+ languages. “Grammar Assistant” to help refine scripts before synthesis. Pitch, speed, and emphasis control on a per-word or per-sentence basis. Ability to add background music from a royalty-free library. Voice Changer: Upload a home recording and turn it into a professional AI voice. Pros: Excellent for collaborative team projects with built-in workspace sharing. The visual timeline editor makes syncing audio to video much easier than using a CLI or raw API. Cons: The voice library is high-quality but lacks the extreme “vocal fry” and texture found in ElevenLabs. Free plan is very restrictive (no downloads allowed). Security & compliance: GDPR, SOC 2, and data encryption. SSO available for Enterprise users. Support & community: Responsive chat support, dedicated account managers for enterprise, and a robust library of tutorials. 3 — Play.ht Play.ht is a versatile platform known for its massive library of voices and its strong integration with content management systems like WordPress. It is designed for bloggers and media companies who want to “audiolize” their written content. Key features: Access to over 900+ AI voices across 142 languages. Integrated WordPress plugin to automatically convert blog posts to audio. “Voice Generation API” for high-scale programmatic audio creation. Support for SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) for fine-tuned control. Real-time streaming API with sub-300ms latency. Distribution tools to push newsletters and blogs to Spotify or iTunes. Pros: One of the largest selections of regional accents and languages in the market. Highly generous commercial rights—you own the audio you create forever. Cons: Interface can feel slightly cluttered due to the massive volume of voices. Quality varies between their “standard” and “ultra-realistic” voice sets. Security & compliance: GDPR compliant, encryption at rest, and secure API keys. Support & community: 24/7 email support, detailed API documentation, and an active user forum. 4 — Lovo.ai (Genny) Lovo.ai, through its flagship platform Genny, focuses on the creative professional. It combines TTS with a suite of AI tools like image generation and scriptwriting, making it a “one-stop shop” for video content creators. Key features: Genny: An all-in-one platform for video editing and voiceover. “Emotional Voices” that can be toggled between 25+ different emotional states. AI Art Generator to create visuals for the synthesized audio. Scriptwriting assistant powered by large language models. Producer mode for granular control over phonemes and pauses. 500+ voices in 100+ languages. Pros: Excellent “Character” voices (ideal for gaming or animation). Affordable entry-level pricing for independent creators. Cons: Some of the standard voices can still sound a bit “processed” compared to the high-tier models. The all-in-one interface can be a bit much if you only need the TTS component. Security & compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, and standard data protection. Support & community: Helpful blog, video tutorials, and active Facebook user group. 5 — Amazon Polly Amazon Polly is the enterprise-standard API for developers. Part of AWS, it focuses on massive scale, low cost, and deep integration with existing cloud infrastructure. Key features: Neural TTS (NTTS) technology for high-quality, natural-sounding speech. “Brand Voice” feature: AWS can help a company build a unique, exclusive voice. Real-time streaming and asynchronous batch processing. Support for “Speech Marks” to synchronize lip-sync in avatars. Low, pay-as-you-go pricing model. Integration with AWS Lambda and S3 for automated workflows. Pros: Extremely reliable and scalable—built for millions of requests per second. The most cost-effective solution for high-volume developers. Cons: Voices are professional but can lack the emotional “spark” of creator-focused tools. Requires technical knowledge of the AWS ecosystem to set up effectively. Security & compliance: HIPAA eligible, PCI DSS, SOC 1/2/3, ISO 27001, and GDPR. Support & community: Enterprise-grade AWS support plans, global developer community, and extensive whitepapers. 6 — Google Cloud Text-to-Speech Google leverages its DeepMind WaveNet technology to provide highly accurate and clear voices. It is particularly strong in language diversity and is the backend for many Google Assistant features. Key features: Powered by DeepMind’s WaveNet and Neural2 models. Selection of over 380+ voices across 50+ languages and variants. Custom Voice: Create a unique voice model for your brand. Linear 16-bit, MP3, or OGG Opus output formats. Dynamic range compression to improve audio quality on small speakers. Seamless integration with other Google Cloud AI tools (Translate, Speech-to-Text). Pros: Exceptional accuracy in pronunciation, especially for complex technical terms. Deep penetration in the global market with excellent non-English voice quality. Cons: No built-in “studio” interface for non-developers; primarily API-based. The pricing model can be confusing (Standard vs. WaveNet vs. Neural2 characters). Security & compliance: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), SOC 1/2/3, HIPAA, and GDPR. Support & community: Extensive documentation, Stack Overflow support, and Google Cloud training modules. 7 — Microsoft Azure AI Speech Microsoft’s TTS solution is widely regarded as the most “flexible” enterprise platform. It offers incredible customization and a wide array of “Styles” (like “cheerful,” “empathetic,” or “newscast”). Key features: Over 400 neural voices across 140 languages and locales. “Speaking Styles” toggle to change the tone of voice based on context. Custom Neural Voice: Create highly realistic, unique voices for enterprise. SSML support for control over rate, pitch, and intonation. Disfluency support (adding “um” and “ah” for extreme realism). Integrated with Microsoft 365 and Azure’s broader AI suite. Pros: The “Styles” feature is the best in the industry for professional narration. Strongest security and compliance for government and highly regulated sectors. Cons: Azure Portal interface is complex and geared toward IT professionals. Setup for “Custom Neural Voice” requires a significant amount of data and manual review. Security & compliance: FedRAMP, HIPAA, ISO, SOC 2, and GDPR. Support & community: Microsoft Learn, Azure forums, and 24/7 enterprise support. 8 — WellSaid Labs WellSaid Labs positions itself as the “ethical” and “corporate” voice platform. They focus on providing a small, highly curated library of perfect voices rather than thousands of mediocre ones. Key features: “Studio” for collaborative team editing. Curated library of professional-sounding voices optimized for training and corporate comms. API for integration into internal LMS (Learning Management Systems). Custom “pronunciation” library to handle industry jargon. High-quality WAV downloads. Real-time rendering. Pros: The most “natural” voices for corporate training and internal communications. Ethical sourcing: All voices are based on real voice actors who are compensated fairly. Cons: Much more expensive than competitors like Play.ht. Smaller voice library compared to the hundreds offered by Google or Microsoft. Security & compliance: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, and secure data hosting. Support & community: High-touch support, dedicated success managers, and clear onboarding. 9 — Speechify Originally an accessibility tool for those with dyslexia, Speechify has evolved into a powerful TTS platform for productivity and content creation. It is unique for its “celebrity voices” and focus on speed-reading. Key features: Celebrity voices like Snoop Dogg and Gwyneth Paltrow. OCR (Optical Character Recognition): Take a photo of a book and it reads it to you. High-speed reading (up to 900wpm) with high comprehension. Browser extensions for Chrome and Safari to read any webpage. Mobile app (iOS/Android) for listening on the go. AI Voiceover studio for video creators. Pros: The best tool for personal productivity and accessibility. Extremely user-friendly interface that feels like a consumer app, not a dev tool. Cons: Subscription cost is quite high compared to other consumer tools. Voice cloning and professional tools are a separate, newer part of their ecosystem. Security & compliance: Standard SSL, GDPR compliant. Support & community: Fast in-app chat support and a massive community of students and professionals. 10 — OpenAI (TTS API) OpenAI, the creators of ChatGPT, recently entered the TTS market with their “tts-1” and “tts-1-hd” models. It is built for simplicity and is incredibly easy to integrate for developers already using the OpenAI API. Key features: Six distinct built-in voices: Alloy, Echo, Fable, Onyx, Nova, and Shimmer. Two model variants: “tts-1” (low latency) and “tts-1-hd” (high quality). Simple API structure with very few parameters to manage. Optimized for conversational AI and real-time feedback. Multi-language support through their Whisper-based architecture. Pros: Easiest API to implement for modern web developers. Very natural, pleasant-sounding default voices with minimal “AI artifacting.” Cons: Extremely limited customization; you cannot adjust pitch, speed, or emphasis via parameters yet. Only six voices available; no voice cloning features for the public API. Security & compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, and optional data exclusion for model training. Support & community: Massive developer community, OpenAI forums, and comprehensive documentation. Which TTS Tool Is Right for You? Solo Users vs. SMB vs. Mid-Market vs. Enterprise Solo Users/Freelancers: Speechify is excellent for personal productivity, while ElevenLabs or Lovo.ai offer the best creative tools for low-budget video production. SMBs: Murf.ai and Play.ht provide the right balance of a user-friendly studio and professional rights without needing a developer on staff. Enterprise: Microsoft Azure or WellSaid Labs are the most appropriate. Azure provides the security and compliance large corporations need, while WellSaid provides the high-end consistency for internal global communications. Budget-Conscious vs. Premium Solutions Budget: Amazon Polly and Google Cloud are the cheapest, but they require technical skills. MailerLite or OpenAI’s API are also very cost-effective for developers. Premium: ElevenLabs and WellSaid Labs are the “Tesla” of TTS. You pay more, but the voices are noticeably superior and less likely to be identified as “AI” by listeners. Feature Depth vs. Ease of Use If you want Ease of Use, stick to Speechify or Murf.ai. You can be up and running in five minutes. If you want Feature Depth (cloning, emotional control, phoneme editing), go with ElevenLabs or Azure AI. Integration and Scalability Needs For developers building a new app from scratch, the OpenAI TTS API or Amazon Polly are the easiest to integrate and scale to millions of users. For those needing to integrate with an existing WordPress site, Play.ht is the clear winner. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. Is AI-generated speech legal for commercial use? In most cases, yes, provided you have a paid subscription. Tools like Murf.ai and ElevenLabs grant full commercial rights to paid users. Always check the terms of service, as free tiers often exclude commercial usage. 2. Can AI voices really replicate emotions like crying or laughing? Platforms like ElevenLabs and Azure AI are getting very close. While they might not “burst into tears,” they can certainly adopt a “sad” tone or add a “laughing” cadence to the speech through emotional style toggles. 3. What is the difference between “Standard” and “Neural” voices? Standard voices use older concatenative technology (stitching audio fragments together). Neural voices use deep learning to generate the waveform from scratch, resulting in much smoother, more human-like speech. 4. How does voice cloning work? You upload a clean audio sample of a person speaking. The AI analyzes the unique frequencies, accents, and quirks of that person’s voice to create a digital model that can then say any text you input. 5. Are these platforms compliant with data privacy laws? The top-tier platforms (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, ElevenLabs) are all GDPR compliant. For medical use, Microsoft and Amazon offer HIPAA-eligible configurations to protect patient data. 6. Can I use these tools to create audiobooks? Absolutely. Many creators use ElevenLabs or WellSaid Labs for this. However, be aware of character limits and cost, as a 10-hour audiobook can require hundreds of thousands of characters. 7. Does TTS work for languages other than English? Yes. Most platforms now support 30 to 140+ languages. Google and Microsoft typically have the best support for less common dialects and non-Western languages. 8. What is SSML? SSML stands for Speech Synthesis Markup Language. It’s a way to “code” your text to tell the AI exactly when to pause, which words to emphasize, and how to pronounce specific names. 9. Will AI voices replace human voice actors? While AI is replacing humans for routine tasks (IVR, internal training, quick YouTube videos), high-stakes dramatic acting, high-budget commercials, and unique brand personalities still heavily favor human performers. 10. What is the “latency” in TTS? Latency is the time between sending a request and hearing the audio. For a “talking AI” chatbot, you need ultra-low latency (under 500ms). For a video voiceover, latency doesn’t matter as much as quality. Conclusion The Text-to-Speech landscape in 2026 is no longer about finding a tool that works—it’s about finding the tool that best fits your specific voice. If your priority is emotional depth and realism, ElevenLabs is currently unmatched. For enterprise-grade reliability and control, Microsoft Azure remains the gold standard. Meanwhile, developers looking for speed and simplicity will find the OpenAI TTS API to be a breath of fresh air. Choosing the right tool ultimately depends on whether you value a visual studio interface or a powerful API, and whether you need 1,000 voices or just one perfect, custom-cloned voice. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.00:59 Samsung Unpacked 2024: New folding phones, Galaxy Watch Ultra unveiledEric Chou, Head of Mobile eXperience, Samsung Electronics Australia talks about the new AI-powered...morelessToggle full description viewSamsung’s next generation of AI will power the biggest changes we have seen in its flagship folding devices as well as a new high end watch, a ring to monitor your sleep, snoring and heart health and earbuds offering better sound and clearer calls.The fun factor is a big feature of the Galaxy Z Flip6 with buzz cases that light up while the larger Galaxy Z Fold6 promises to take productivity, gaming and entertainment to the next level through a slimmer, lighter and squarer design.At 239 grams, it’s only a few grams heavier than the S24Ultra despite its impressive 7.6-inch display offering 374 pixels per inch and an 120Hz adaptive refresh rate. Samsung Unpacked 2024, held in Paris, featured the release of a high end 3000 nit bright Galaxy Watch Ultra which promises to give triathletes, marathon runners and future Olympians everything they need to monitor their performance. One of the biggest changes is in the design of the new Buds and Buds Pro which now feature a ‘blade’, similar to the look of Apple’s AirPods, to provide clearer calls and more advanced AI translation features.Galaxy Watch Ultra has been launched as part of Samsung Unpacked in Paris.Samsung says Australians are among the fastest adopters of AI in the world with 80 per cent of S24 phone users using new features introduced at the first Unpacked event in January this year. The next generation of AI in Fold6 will allow everything from quick summaries of articles, continuous transcription in the palm of your hands, as well as being able to generate AI additions to your photos (like a coffee mug on a desk) by just drawing on them.Samsung Galaxy Z Flip6 does some cool watercolours and 3D cartoons with your portraits. The benefits of a larger folding screen become obvious as you watch demonstrations of the original text in another language on one screen and the translation on another. Portrait Studio is another AI-powered feature which will allow you to generate 3D cartoons or watercolours from your photos. Live translation of phone calls, even in third party apps, will bring down communication barriers even further, something that will appeal to travellers or those doing business across the world.Samsung's new pink Galaxy Z Fold6 and silver Galaxy Watch Ultra.One of the key upgrades to the more affordable Flip6 is a new 50MP wide and 12MP ultra-wide sensors on the cameras.With the new Auto zoom, FlexCam automatically finds the best framing for your shot by detecting the subject and zooming in and out before making any necessary adjustments. It’s almost like having your own AI camera operator, something that will no doubt appeal to content creators, influencers and vloggers.The camera offers 2x optical quality zoom and up to 10 times with AI.AUSSIE ACCENT AND SLAGSamsung is particularly proud of the thousands of hours that have been put in by its local staff to cater for the Australian accent and our use of slang.While artificial intelligence is a big reason people are switching to Samsung phones, the tech giant acknowledges not everyone is at ease with the technology. Many, but not all, of Samsung’s AI functionality is done on device but it says users will have the option to switch off AI where they want through a dashboard to protect their privacy. Samsung also has its own Knox security system to help protect personal information.Galaxy Buds3 have a new blade design which includes its own light.About 70 per cent of users are using AI on a monthly basis with circle to search and chat assist being among popular features in Australia. Samsung says it will continue to develop AI technology with upgrades also being made to previous models.AI functionality will even be available on its cheaper phone models though the offering will be limited due to the slower processors.COULD AI END UP COSTING US?While free until the end of 2025, Samsung acknowledges that some AI services in the future could require a subscription if partners like Microsoft and Google start charging.Eric Chou, Head of Mobile eXperience, Samsung Electronics Australia, said the company would continue to invest heavily in AI to lead the way for its customers.“We’re pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with AI-driven features in smartphones and wearables, offering our users enhanced functionality, improved durability, and cutting-edge design,’’ Mr Chou said.The colour line up for the Galaxy Z Fold6 from Samsung.Nathan Rigger, Head of Mobile Product, said the sixth generation Z foldables followed 13 years of hard work and innovation. “With Galaxy AI on the Galaxy Z Flip6 and Fold6, we’re delivering incredible AI-driven features and performance, in the sleekest and strongest foldable designs we’ve ever produced.” Kylie Mason, Head of Wearables and Accessories, described the watch and accessories line-up as the biggest improvement she had seen in her years at Samsung.Galaxy Watch Ultra an ‘exciting leap forward’.“Galaxy Watch Ultra represents an exciting leap forward for active Australians who push the boundaries of achievement,’’ Ms Mason said.“With our most significant hardware and software advancements to date, it features drastically improved accuracy and performance to better meet Australians’ needs.“Whether you are an elite athlete, an outdoor addict or simply someone who values health and wellness, the Watch Ultra is the ultimate companion for those who demand the best.”GALAXY Z FOLD6Key features include: Note Assist on Samsung Notes offers translation, summaries, and auto formatting for easy meeting notes. A newly embedded transcript feature enables transcription, translation and summarising of voice recordings directly in Notes. Texts in PDF files can be translated and overlaid through the PDF overlay translation. It also supports text in images and graphs. Composer generates text based on simple keywords for emails, social media posts and comments. Samsung's new Galaxy Z Fold6.Sketch to Image, draw virtually anywhere and create AI-generated images. With Circle to Search, you can long press the home button and circle on a video to search who the artist is.Interpreter comes with a conversation mode that enables both parties to view translations on the main and cover screens for more natural interactions. It also offers one-way translation, so you can easily understand when listening during lectures or any other type of presentation. Galaxy Z Flip6 features an auto zoom mode.Through Live Translate phone calls are directly translated on your device in real-time.Advanced editing experience with Photo Assist on the large screen helps to create professional-grade content. Portrait Studio creates a variety of different portrait styles such as 3D cartoon or watercolour.Instant Slow-mo allows you to instantly slow a video by generating additional frames. You also have the option of saving and sharing your videos with friends and familyGalaxy Z Fold6 offers an upgraded gaming experience with a 1.6x larger vapour chamber for the ability to game for longer, while maintaining performance. page_title: The Best Japanese Translation Apps For Japan Travel - Inside Kyoto
meta_description: Can Japanese translation apps help you during your Japan travels? We've tested 5 Japanese translation apps in real life Japan: here's our in-depth guide.
content: Concerned about communicating in Japan? Make your travels in Japan as smooth and hassle-free as possible with a translation app. Discover the translation apps we’ve tested in real life and find out which ones actually work with our in-depth guide. Six translation apps for Japan travel © Florentyna Leow One of the most intimidating things about traveling somewhere new like Japan used to be language barriers – being unable to communicate your needs and wants to people, or indeed understand anything they were saying to you. Fortunately, you won’t need to slip Douglas Adams’ small, yellow, leech-like Babel Fish into your ear to understand what anyone’s saying on your travels. Instead, you can use today’s modern equivalent on your smartphone to communicate with locals: a translation app. In this guide, we show you some of the best translation apps out there for traveling in Japan. By ‘best’ we mean useful and practical – translation apps are never 100% accurate, but they’re fantastic for breaking down those language barriers. This guide contains the following sections: Using iPhone’s Built-in Translation App Japanese–English and English–Japanese Translation Apps for iPhones What makes a useful travel app? Test-driving translation apps for Japan travel – Text translation – Image translation – Voice translation Final thoughts Practical Kyoto Kyoto ItinerariesMake the most of your trip with tailored Kyoto itinerariesMore InfoGuide To Japan EntryFull guide to the recommended Visit Japan Web appMore InfoPacking List For JapanComprehensive checklist to make sure you take what you needMore InfoWhere To Stay In KyotoOur guide to Kyoto’s key areas for places to stayMore Info First: iPhones Built-in Text Translation Feature If you’ve got a relatively new iPhone, you already have the most useful and user-friendly text translation app in your pocket. Because it’s built into the operating system, it requires no installation or configuration. Here’s how to use it: Point your camera at the text you want to translate. Here, we’ll use a typical café menu to demonstrate. Menu to be translated seen through iPhone The camera will detect any text within the frame. It will indicate the text with yellow brackets around the text. Brackets appear around text This text will pop up into a new “window” within the photo. If it doesn’t, you can tap the bracketed text. Selected text pops up A “Translate” button pops up near the bottom of the window. Tap this button. Translation button appears The translated text appears in your window. Translated text appears In addition to translating through your camera, you can also open any photo in your Photos folder and use the same process to translate any Japanese text in that photo. Now, if you want to use a stand-alone translation app, read on for our review of the best ones out there. Spoiler: It’s not 100% accurate, but out of all the apps I tested, Photo Translator performed best with handwritten menus © Florentyna Leow Japanese–English and English–Japanese Translation Apps for iPhones There are quite literally hundreds of translation apps out there. The goal was to find useful, intuitive apps that non-Japanese speakers could use to communicate with locals, figure out what’s what, and generally get around. For this reason, I didn’t include grammar-focused Japanese-learning apps, ‘phrasebook’ apps, or dictionary apps. I took six translation apps out into the Tokyo wilderness for a spin. These were downloaded from the App Store on an iPhone, though some of these will also be available on Android. I’ve noted wherever this is the case. In no particular order, these are the apps I tested: 1. Google Translate There are three main parts to this app: photo, voice, and text translation. Using this app, you point your phone camera at the text you want to read, and the optical character recognition (OCR) technology “reads” the text and displays the translation directly on your phone screen, displacing the original text. You can also type in English text that will be translated into Japanese (or other languages) and vice versa. There’s also an option to speak into the phone’s inbuilt microphone. Google Translate records and renders your words into text, then produces a translation. This is then read out to you in the target language. Google Translate also works offline. It’s available on iOS and Android (but of course) and is free for use. 2. Waygo This app allows you to write or ‘draw’ kanji characters onto the screen. This does rely on some prior knowledge of Japanese, Chinese, or Korean characters. You are also able to hold the phone up to a given text or set of words and have Waygo render a translation. The app limits you to 10 free translations a day; beyond this, you’ll need to purchase the app. Available on iOS. There’s also an official website. 3. iTranslate This app offers text, voice, and photo translation. While you can translate between English and Japanese, there are around 40 language pairs available. As a bonus, it works offline once you’ve downloaded the requisite language packs. I tested this with a free trial of the paid version. Available on iOS and Android. 4. PapaGo Developed by Naver, this app does text, voice, and photo translation. It also allows you to have a simultaneous conversation in two languages using the app. You’ll be passing the phone back and forth between you and another person speaking a different language into the phone. PapaGo also translates between various Asian languages, including Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, and Chinese. If you’re traveling around Asia, you might want to check this out. You will need to be connected to the internet to use this app, but on the bright side, it’s free. Available on iOS and Android. 5. Japanese Translator Offline In this app, you’ll type in the sentence you need and it spits out a Japanese rendering for you. You can also speak into the app. As the name suggests, you won’t need WiFi to use this. It’s a free app. At this point in time, to our knowledge, this is iOS only. 6. Photo Translator + + This is the companion app to Japanese Translation, also by Evolly.app. You can either upload a photo with Japanese text from your camera library or take a photo of what you’re looking at, and it will give you a translation superimposed on top of the original text. This particular free app will require you to watch the occasional video ad (30 seconds at most, and usually about 10 seconds), but it’s a small price to pay. Available on iOS and Android. A handwritten drinks menu I tried the apps on © Florentyna Leow What makes a useful Japanese translation travel app? The real test, of course, is: a) how practical they are when you’re actually traveling around Japan b) how useful they are for communicating c) how easy and intuitive the apps themselves are to use. I’ve compared these apps by their respective functions. These are a few of the criteria I considered when testing the apps: Text translation: If I typed in English sentences, would they be translated into accurate or understandable Japanese? Similarly, if a native Japanese speaker typed in something, would the English rendering be accurate? Image translation: How good is the app at deciphering and capturing Japanese text? Would the app be able to render this text into understandable English? Could the app read handwritten menus and signs? Voice translation: How accurately can the app decipher English-language sentences spoken into the phone? How accurate were the Japanese translations of our words? Would this be as accurate for Japanese speakers? Test-Driving Japanese Translation Apps for Japan Travel Using Google Translate’s text input © Florentyna Leow Text Translation Google Translate has improved in leaps and bounds over the last few years, which is evident in the above-average quality of its translations. It does reasonably well with sentences a traveler might potentially ask. For the best results – and this is true of all the apps below – you want to communicate in simple sentences that leave no room for ambiguity. In the same way, Japanese to English translations work best with uncomplicated sentences and concepts. You might not be having deep, philosophical conversations with another local – unless you’re willing to sit down for a good length of time – but you will at least find out where the nearest bathroom is. Using iTranslate Pro’s text input © Florentyna Leow iTranslate fared decently, though the translations that emerge aren’t always 100% correct. For instance, in the middle example, the word for “top up” is translated to “上げる” or “raise,” which doesn’t make any sense in Japanese. Contextually, someone might eventually understand it. If you receive a puzzled look in return when you show them a translated sentence, your intended meaning might have been lost in translation, so consider rephrasing. Something else I noticed with iTranslate is that it does not always perform well with compound sentences. The third sentence above has two parts: defining ‘warabimochi’ and asking if it’s vegan. The translation that emerged only translated the first half of the sentence and not the second. This is something that can happen with translation apps generally, so you’ll want to keep your queries and statements short and simple. Using Japanese Translator Offline © Florentyna Leow As expected of an app specializing in Japanese–English translations, this performed well. The interface is clean and straightforward. The Japanese translations the app gives you are generally on the formal side, but that’s an observation rather than a complaint. It’s great for casual travelers. But, this is also a useful app for beginner to intermediate learners of Japanese, as you’ll see not only what you wanted translated, but also similar example sentences to reinforce your learning. Additionally, it’s worth mentioning that Japanese Translator Offline is good at capturing sentences spoken into the app – I tested all the examples above by typing and speaking them in. It works well with Japanese-language input too. Text translations for PapaGo © Florentyna Leow Not only were they accurate, PapaGos’s Japanese translations of our text-based queries were some of the most natural-sounding out of all the apps we used. They won’t always be ‘formal’ but they sound like someone you might actually hear talking on the street, which is a nice bonus. The app itself is also easy to use, with colour-coded and easily understandable functions. Image Translation Reading text on a Dyson vacuum cleaner box with Google Translate © Florentyna Leow I had high hopes for Google Translate’s much-feted Word Lens. I trained the phone camera on printed text on the side of a Dyson vacuum cleaner box to reasonably clear results. The translation wasn’t perfect – the first sentence is more accurately rendered as “Continuing to challenge even with repeated failures” – but the technology itself is impressive. Four instances of using Google Translate in the wild © Florentyna Leow Word Lens produces decent on-the-spot translations when you hover over clear, printed text. But you have mixed results in various real-life situations. The menu on the left is imperfectly translated, and the non-Japanese reader would be hard-pressed to order from it, though the app did its best with the vertical text. The third example above (second to right) shows Word Lens trying to interpret a handwritten menu. In general, the app does not do well (yet) hovering over handwritten text regardless of legibility, so it’s not useful in many Japanese restaurants. It does better when you take a photo of something and use the app to read it from your library. Still, if you just want to figure out what flavour of chocolate you’re buying from the convenience store (far right), Google Translate’s photo function doesn’t do too badly. Using Waygo in the wild © Florentyna Leow For all the praise it has received for its East Asia-specific character recognition, Waygo was surprisingly unhelpful when it came to practical use in Japan. It was able to read some printed text but not most things I trained the camera on, whether handwritten, printed, vertical, or horizontal. More instances of using Waygo. From left to right: a sandwich board, a handwritten menu, a train ticket, and an entrance ticket to the Golden Pavilion © Florentyna Leow In more cases than not, it was unable to detect any text or find any translations for the text I looked at. There was just one occasion where it managed to translate something accurately! The OCR technology just was not up to par with some of the other apps I tried out. Waygo is purportedly useful for language learners in East Asia when it comes to identifying kanji characters, especially in China. But if you’re looking for a straightforward and intuitive translation app for Japan travel, Waygo isn’t it – especially not with just 10 free translations a day. Given the existence of other better apps out there, you can skip this. Reading a handwritten sign. A rough translation is: “A request to customers. When it is busy and when you are queuing, please stand close to the person in front of you as much as possible. Please cooperate for queuing. Thank you” © Florentyna Leow With PapaGo’s photo translation function, you point your phone camera at a scene or text that you want to read. Once you snap a photo, the app scans it for any text and highlights any Japanese text in white outlined box. You can then tap on each highlighted box to read what it says. To its credit, PapaGo performs much better than Google Translate when it comes to deciphering handwritten text, even if what comes out is barely understandable or outright inaccurate. The middle translation is just on the mark; the second should read “please cooperate and queue.” More instances of using PapaGo in the wild © Florentyna Leow The left translation should have read “mutton keema” towards the end, and 温玉 is an onsen egg rather than a “hot ball” – but it’s possible to at least get an idea of what’s on the menu, even if it’s written on a chalkboard in vertical text. Also, ‘salmon-bashing warship’ is a direct translation of what’s written there, even if it actually refers to gunkan-style sushi with chopped salmon. iTranslate’s results are a mixed bag when it comes to image translations © Florentyna Leow Out of all the apps here, iTranslate proved the least useful for image translations. Sometimes it wouldn’t be able to detect any printed text in the image, and when it did, it wasn’t the most pleasant to read. If you tried to move the borders of the white box on the screen, your translation would disappear. It’s not the most intuitive app around. Reading a drinks menu – it’s not half bad © Florentyna Leow Photo Translator was the surprise winner in the battle of photo translation here. You won’t go thirsty with the drinks menu in front of you, for one thing. It helps to first take a photo of what you want to decipher and upload it to the app from your library. Translating the entrance ticket to the Temple of the Golden Pavilion © Florentyna Leow I wasn’t seriously expecting the app to be able to read the ticket you receive from the Temple of the Golden Pavilion in Kyoto. The translation that came out wasn’t really accurate, but it does give you a sense of what’s on the ticket. Reading gas bills and information from TEPCO © Florentyna Leow In general, though, this app out-performed even Google Translate when it came to reading and translating more complex texts. If you ever have to read longer printed sentences in Japanese, this is the app to use. Voice Translation Testing Google Translate’s voice recognition software © Florentyna Leow Google Translate’s voice recognition is surprisingly good. It picks up English sentences accurately as long as you speak quite clearly, and the resulting translations are fine. It worked with a Malaysian accent, too. Testing simple sentences with PapaGo © Florentyna Leow PapaGo’s voice recognition also works well for simple English sentences that a traveler might ask about directions and food allergies. Though it ultimately doesn’t make too much difference, PapaGo’s Japanese (female) voice rings clear and cheerful. Coupled with the bright green background and large, clear text, the app is just that much more fun to use than the others mentioned here. A number of sentence tests with JTO © Florentyna Leow Japanese Translator Offline managed to capture all the sentences above into the microphone on the first go – I liked this app a lot. While not pictured, it also performs admirably for Japanese-language input. Testing both English and Japanese-language voice recognition © Florentyna Leow iTranslate works fine in English in most cases, though the Japanese-language input leaves a little bit to be desired. (The sentences should have captured and translated: “Sorry, everything contains dashi” and “Sorry, we can’t remove the dashi.”) The onus will be on the Japanese local to get this right, however! Comparing voice recognition software on three apps © Florentyna Leow I did a comparison of the same phrase across three of the apps above. They produced accurate if slightly different translations. In this case, PapaGo’s rendering was the most natural, using Japanese that the average speaker would most likely use. However, all of them get the point across. Trying to ask for directions to the inn © Florentyna Leow What is so far true across all the apps I tested, though, is that they’re not great at picking up Japanese words mixed in with English sentences. ‘Ryokan,’ which refers to a Japanese-style inn, proved to be a good test for the voice recognition function – it’s not easy for non-Japanese speakers to pronounce accurately. The first three sentences from PapaGo above resulted from attempts to ask for directions to the ryokan – “real kind” was possibly the closest it came. Saying it in Japanese, on the other hand, produced perfectly understandable results. Asking for directions to the inn © Florentyna Leow This was also true of Google Translate’s voice recognition, though it outperforms PapaGo in these terms if you’re willing to try a few times. It took several attempts for it to understand that I was saying ‘ryokan’ instead of ‘dokkan,’ ‘Yukon,’ ‘know you can,’ and other variants. Testing out Japanese words mixed into English sentences © Florentyna Leow I also asked a friend to say some sentences with Japanese words mixed in to the English. To wit, the original sentences spoken into PapaGo above were: 1) I need a bowl of sukiyaki (beef and vegetables cooked in soy, sugar, and sake) 2) Where is the kissaten (a retro Japanese-style cafe) 3) I would like the tempura please. Asking for directions to Meiji-jingumae Station © Florentyna Leow When it came to asking for directions to Meiji-jingumae Station, only Google Translate managed to pick up something approximate. The rest of the apps didn’t quite pan out. (One of the attempts with Japanese Translator Offline came out with the chuckle-inducing “which way to make you think of my station.”) Why should this be the case? The short answer is that the technology for machines to recognize several languages in a single sentence just hasn’t reached the point where it can displace multilingual humans. (On the bright side, it means that interpreters won’t be out of a job just yet.) What this means for an app user: for best results, speak clearly, in simple English-only sentences with key words that communicate exactly what you’re trying to say. If you have place names or particular words in Japanese you want to say, a typed translation is likely to give you better results than a spoken one. Japanese-only menus become a great deal more approachable with translation apps – up to a point © Florentyna Leow Final thoughts Is there a particular app I would recommend? meta_description: Tip: Compare your options, check out our overview of the live simultaneous translation options. Adding closed captions or subtitles to...
content: In this article Selecting a captioning proxyCaptions workflow using EEG live captioningFAQ about using EEG closed captions or subtitlesDo captions work with Studio / RTMPS / SpotMe Express / StreamYard / OBS / etc?How many languages can be translated for a single stream?Do live captions work with video breakouts?Are captions available for on-demand videos?Can the generated captions and subtitles be downloaded from Backstage?What kind of delay do captions add to the live stream?How accurate are the captions? Do they work with different accents?Is it possible to caption a session where each speaker speaks in a different language?Do speakers see the live captions in Studio?Are closed captions supported on mobile apps?Can closed captions be used alongside Interprefy line interpretation on the same stream? Tip: Compare your options, check out our overview of the live simultaneous translation options. Adding closed captions or subtitles to your live stream will help you make your live sessions accessible to a much wider audience. Subtitles appear in text format in real-time on the screen during the live stream, detailing exactly what the speakers are saying. SpotMe Streaming (RTMPS), SpotMe Studio, and SpotMe Express webinars allow you to display captions for the language spoken in the video, as well as translated subtitles in up to 3 other languages. Once the subtitles are enabled in Backstage on your live stream, your attendees will be able to choose whether or not to display the subtitles in the app, and select the language they prefer out of those made available. Note: Closed captions are supported on both the web app and the mobile app. Tip: Take a look at our FAQ section at the bottom of this article for more information on how closed captioning work on the SpotMe platform. Selecting a captioning proxy SpotMe Streaming and Studio support captions use the CC-608 standard on our RTMP and RTMPS endpoints for live streams. Please reach out to your SpotMe contact to help you set-up closed captions. In the meantime though, below you will find more information on how this works, as well as a dedicated FAQ. Captions workflow using EEG live captioning The below flow chart provides a breakdown of how the different components work together as part of adding subtitles to your SpotMe live stream using EEG live captioning. Here you can see that there are five main steps involved: Connect the SpotMe live stream to the EEG live captioning platform. Create the source (or spoken) language captions from the live stream audio, in EEG Lexi. Translate the source captions into multiple target languages, using EEG iCap. Add and synchronize the captions and translated subtitles with the live stream, using EEG Falcon. Send the live stream back into SpotMe, with the available captions/subtitles added for your audience to choose from. FAQ about using EEG closed captions or subtitles Do captions work with Studio / RTMPS / SpotMe Express / StreamYard / OBS / etc? Captions work regardless of which broadcasting software is being used. This works because captions are generated in the cloud from the audio of the live stream that is being sent by the broadcasting software to our captioning service. How many languages can be translated for a single stream? A live stream can have up to 4 captions or subtitles. One subtitle channel is used for the original (spoken) language and the remaining three can be used for translations. This a technical limitation of the standard used for live streaming captions (CC-608). 1 language for the closed captions of the (single) spoken language: English (US, UK, AU)Spanish (Mexico)French (France, Canada)GermanItalianPortuguese (Brazil) Up to 3 languages for the subtitle translations: EnglishDanishGermanSpanishFinnishFrenchItalianMaoriNorwegianPortugueseSwedish Do live captions work with video breakouts? Captions do not work with video breakouts. A user can however use alternative tools for breakouts, such as Google Chrome’s Live Captions. Are captions available for on-demand videos? Captions generated during a live stream are automatically available for the replay of that live stream once it is published on SpotMe. Can the generated captions and subtitles be downloaded from Backstage? No, captions cannot be downloaded from Backstage. What kind of delay do captions add to the live stream? Captioning adds an additional ~10 seconds of delay to the live stream. This brings the total live stream delay to around 40 seconds. How accurate are the captions? Do they work with different accents? EEG estimates up to 96% accuracy rate for the generated captions. While the machine-learning models used to transcribe the text are trained on a wide set of voices and accents, it’s not possible to guarantee that captioning will work the same way for everyone. To improve the captions accuracy, here are a few general tips for speakers: Use a good quality microphone in a room with no background noise. If you are a fast talker, try speaking a bit slower than usual and pronounce words clearly. Have just one person talking at a time. The closed caption accuracy can be improved by adding industry/specialized jargon to the system language model (for example acronyms or brand names), to help the tool recognize those words. Is it possible to caption a session where each speaker speaks in a different language? Sessions with people speaking multiple languages are not supported. For captioning to work everyone in the session needs to speak the same language. For cases were speakers speak different languages, we recommend using Interprefy instead. Do speakers see the live captions in Studio? Speakers and event organizers do not see live captions in Studio. They are only visible to attendees in the web app. This is because captions are added in the cloud, after Studio sends the composed audio from all of speakers to the captioning service. For speakers that need to see captions in the Studio, we recommend using Google Chrome’s Live Captions. Are closed captions supported on mobile apps? Yes, captions are supported on the SpotMe web app and mobile app, using SpotMe Anywhere, SpotMe Express and SpotMe Content Hub. Can closed captions be used alongside Interprefy line interpretation on the same stream? Closed captions can be enabled together on the same live session with Interprefy live interpretation. page_title: Apple brings Live Translation to iMessage, phone calls, and more
meta_description: Apple is breaking down language barriers with a new Live Translation feature in iOS 26 powered by the company's on-device AI processing models.
content: Apple is breaking down language barriers with a new Live Translation feature in iOS 26 powered by the company's on-device AI processing models. The Live Translation feature, announced during the company's WWDC 2025 event, brings real-time language translation to iOS 26. The feature will work across Messages, FaceTime, and other apps. For example, the Live Translation feature can immediately translate text into other languages as you type out a message in iMessage. As texts in other languages come in, the Apple Intelligence feature can instantly translate them for you. Apple says that the new feature works seamlessly across its first-party apps, even if the person you're talking to isn't using an iPhone. Additionally, Apple also announced a Call Translation API for developers to use in their own third-party apps. Real-time translation is also making its way into non-communications apps later this year, with Apple Music bringing live lyric translation and pronunciation features to its app in iOS 26.

Tim Bajarin covers the tech industry’s impact on PC and CE markets.Follow AuthorFeb 18, 2025, 10:00am ESTReal-time translation via smart devices may revolutionize communication.gettyImagine traveling to a foreign country where you don’t speak the language and trying to communicate. It’s a struggle that many of us have faced—myself included. In 1971, I landed in Paris for the first time, before attending college in Switzerland. As an English speaker, navigating the language barrier was an overwhelming challenge. Fast-forward to today and technology is making what once seemed impossible—real-time language translation—an everyday reality.Smart glasses and smart earbuds are emerging as the key game-changers in overcoming language barriers. These innovative devices, equipped with advanced translation technology, are revolutionizing how we interact with people across different cultures. Now, with smart glasses and earbuds, communicating in any language is becoming seamless, making global travel, business, and even local interactions in multilingual areas more accessible.Innovative Real-Time Translation TechnologyOne of the most groundbreaking aspects of these smart devices is their ability to offer real-time translation. I had a firsthand experience with this technology at CES, where I tried out Even Realities’ Even G1 smart glasses. These glasses can instantly translate spoken words into text displayed directly on the lens, allowing me to converse with a CEO in his native Chinese. With real-time translation in 23 languages and more on the way, the potential of these glasses is staggering. Devices like the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarers and Solos Smart Glasses also incorporate translation technology, making communication with people across different languages as easy as wearing glasses. In fact, in talking with many smart glass makers, real-time language translation is high on their list of products to add as well.Meanwhile, smart earbuds also play a huge role in breaking down language barriers. For example, the Vasco Translator E1 earbuds—capable of translating 51 languages—use AI-driven translation engines. The design is user-friendly, with a focus on sharing between two users. Each person wears a different earbud and has a conversation in real-time. This sharing capability is practical and opens up endless possibilities for cross-cultural communication.There are many language translation earbuds currently on the market. The folks at Buyers Guide reviewed ten of these translation earbuds and awarded their Editor’s Choice to the Timekettle M3 Language Translator earbuds. MORE FOR YOUThe Epstein Files Reveal Jeffrey Epstein Got Banned From Xbox LiveRotten Tomatoes Critics Splatter Melania Trump Documentary With Harsh ReviewsAn Agent Revolt: Moltbook Is Not A Good IdeaHow Real-Time Translation Is Changing Global InteractionThe impact of smart glasses and earbuds on global communication cannot be overstated. Here's a closer look at how these innovations are shaping the world:Real-Time CommunicationSmart glasses and earbuds make it possible for individuals to hold fluid conversations without the need for an interpreter. Whether it's business meetings, social interactions, or casual conversations, these devices can translate speech instantly—displaying the translation as text or delivering it audibly.International Relations and DiplomacyAR translation could strengthen ties between nations by enhancing communication at international gatherings like the United Nations. This technology could potentially reduce the need for professional interpreters, saving time and resources while allowing for more direct and efficient interactions between world leaders and delegates. Travel and TourismTravelers will find these translation devices indispensable. With smart glasses and earbuds, navigating a foreign city, ordering food, or understanding signs becomes hassle-free. These technologies ensure that language barriers no longer limit the travel experience, creating a more inclusive world for globetrotters.Business and CommerceInternational business meetings and negotiations will become more efficient and inclusive. Smart glasses with translation features will enable multilingual group communication in real-time, fostering faster and more effective collaboration across language divides.Education and Language LearningAlthough not replacing formal language education, smart translation devices can be excellent tools for language learners. They offer a unique way to practice and immerse oneself in conversations, provide instant feedback, and help learners adapt to real-world situations.AccessibilityFor deaf or hard-of-hearing individuals, the future of translation-enabled smart glasses holds exciting potential, such as the HearView glasses. With the integration of real-time captioning, these devices could eventually provide an inclusive solution for multilingual communication, making public interactions more accessible to everyone.Challenges and Future PossibilitiesWhile the future of real-time translation technology looks promising, there are still some hurdles to overcome: Translation engines may struggle with idiomatic expressions or slang.Translating conversations with multiple speakers or rapid dialogue can pose challenges.Different accents and dialects may affect translation accuracy. Recording conversations for translation purposes raises potential privacy issues.Despite these challenges, as technology advances, global communication's future looks increasingly interconnected.As someone who has traveled the world and struggled with language barriers, integrating real-time translation technology into smart glasses and earbuds is nothing short of revolutionary. This "killer app" can bridge communication gaps and bring people closer, fostering a deeper understanding between cultures.The potential for smart translation devices to transform international relations, business practices, travel experiences, and education is huge. These technologies are not just enhancing communication but potentially reshaping how we connect with people worldwide. For myself and countless others, this game-changing development will make cross-cultural interactions more meaningful and fulfilling.Disclosure: Meta subscribes to Creative Strategies research reports along with many other high tech companies around the world.Editorial StandardsReprints & PermissionsFind Tim Bajarin on X. content: Top 12 Best AI Transcription Software of 2025 (Ranked)Kate StronachSeptember 29, 2025In a world saturated with audio and video content, manually transcribing meetings, interviews, podcasts, and lectures is no longer a viable option. AI has transformed this once tedious task into a near-instantaneous process, but not all tools are created equal. The market is crowded with platforms offering a wide range of features, from basic speech-to-text to sophisticated AI-powered summaries and content repurposing tools. Choosing the right platform depends heavily on your specific needs, whether it's absolute data privacy, seamless integration into a creative workflow, or enterprise-level compliance for sensitive data. For instance, content marketers and social media professionals need tools that can quickly turn video content into accurate text; modern AI transcription software is also adept at helping creators auto-generate TikTok captions with AI, expanding reach and accessibility on social platforms. Similarly, a legal professional's requirements for security and accuracy will differ vastly from those of a podcaster looking for speaker labels and timestamps.Who Uses AI Transcription Software the Most?PodcastersTurn long recordings into show notes, social captions, episode summaries, and SEO-ready blog content in minutes.Marketing TeamsConvert webinars, interviews, and videos into reusable written assets for ads, posts, and landing pages.Sales TeamsAutomatically capture meeting discussions, objections, and next steps for CRM updates and follow-ups.Educators & StudentsTransform lectures and tutorials into searchable study materials and revision notes.This guide cuts through the marketing noise to provide a detailed, practical comparison of the 12 best AI transcription software options available. We will analyze each tool's core strengths, expose its limitations, and provide clear use-case recommendations. Each entry includes direct links and screenshots to help you find the perfect fit for your workflow, whether you're a solo creator, a fast-moving team, or a large enterprise. This isn't just a list; it's a resource designed to help you make an informed decision and select the most effective solution for turning your audio into actionable, accurate text. 1. Transcript.LOL Transcript.LOL positions itself as a top-tier choice for the best AI transcription software by blending high-end accuracy with an exceptional suite of post-transcription tools. It’s a comprehensive platform built for professionals who need to convert audio and video into more than just text.Core AI Transcription EngineImport from multiple sourcesImport audio and video files from various sources including direct upload, Google Drive, Dropbox, URLs, Zoom, and more.#1 in speech to text accuracyUltra fast resultsCustom vocabulary support10 hours long fileState-of-the-art AIPowered by OpenAI's Whisper for industry-leading accuracy. Support for custom vocabularies, up to 10 hours long files, and ultra fast results.Export in multiple formatsExport your transcripts in multiple formats including TXT, DOCX, PDF, SRT, and VTT with customizable formatting options.By leveraging OpenAI’s Whisper engine, it delivers rapid, near-human accuracy while supporting an impressive range of import options, including direct uploads, cloud drives, and even YouTube links. This flexibility makes it an ideal hub for centralizing all transcription needs.Why Centralized Transcription Saves Hours Every Week?Using multiple transcription tools fragments your workflow and increases errors. A centralized system keeps files, summaries, and exports in one place, reducing tool-switching and speeding up content production from recording to publishing.The platform’s standout feature is its ability to transform raw transcripts into actionable content. Instead of just delivering text, it generates summaries, action items, social media posts, and even mind maps. This turns a simple transcript into a powerful productivity tool, allowing podcasters to create show notes, marketers to draft posts, and corporate teams to extract key decisions from meetings automatically. Core Features & Analysis High-Volume Capacity: Supports file uploads up to 10 hours long (5 GB), making it perfect for long-form content like podcasts, webinars, and lectures. Robust Integrations: Offers a Chrome extension, API access, and connections with Google Drive, Zoom, Zapier, WhatsApp, and Telegram, ensuring it fits into existing processes.
